title: Integration in Memphis and Fisk; touring homecomings with the Collegians
summary: Jones recalls the integrated atmosphere at Le Moine and Fisk and the Collegians' homecoming dates at several universities.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: You mentioned early, when we first started to talk, about when you went back with your father when -- was it Le Moine University honored him?
And you said that it was integrated there. Did you mean at the university or did you mean in the
Oh. It was completely integrated or --
And that would have been, well you said you were about eight or nine years old.

Uh-huh. Because all the homes we went to were -- not all of them, but they respected my father highly. And these were white homes. There was no problem, no nothing. We had a ball, you know? It was no -- nothing like what came up later. Now they say it's really improved greatly. Like at Fisk University, we used to play -- what we would play was -- like with the Collegians, we travelled to all the schools. West Virginia State, Fisk University, and the University of Kentucky. Playing homecomings.

You know? With all the bonfires and the football teams. Oh, that was -- they were some great days, you know? And I went to Fisk University, and they were just as integrated as you want to be, you know?
Yeah, in my day, you know, but my old man had graduated from there. early. you know.
That's how he got his teaching certificate

for Le Moine College. But they were all -- and they treated us beautifully. You'd stay in the dormitory. You'd go to the dining room and eat and hang out with the faculty members and the student body, you know.
And they would all stand around the bandstand and we were young and cocky, you know, and those pretty little girls would make you turn your head around a minute, you know?
